meta.title: Who really said "The more difficult the victory, the greater the happiness in winning"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Pelé really wrote it — but in his 1977 autobiography the line reads "a victory," not "the victory." The primary source, and where the extra word went.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The more difficult the victory, the greater the happiness in winning'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, it's Pelé — traced to his 1977 memoir My Life and the Beautiful Game. But he wrote "a victory," not "the victory." One word off.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Pelé wrote the sentence in his 1977 autobiography, My Life and the Beautiful Game (with Robert L. Fish, Doubleday), in a passage about a World Cup match — but the book reads “the more difficult a victory,” not “the victory.” The line the internet prints is his, with one word swapped.
answer.confidenceText: Verified as Pelé’s own writing — located in the primary source — with one caveat: the memoir says “a victory” where the circulating version says “the victory.”

source.heading: The sentence, in the book that actually contains it

docMeta.dd: My Life and the Beautiful Game: The Autobiography of Pelé
Robert L. Fish, listed in the catalogue record as joint author
Doubleday, Garden City, N.Y., 1977 (1st ed.); reissued by Skyhorse Publishing, 2007
“The more difficult a victory, the greater the happiness in winning.”

source.excerpt: … our Selection, for it ensured our continuing in the World Cup games. The more difficult a victory, the greater the happiness in winning. After the game, back at the hotel, we read and heard on the radio …
trail: 1977 — the memoir. Pelé’s autobiography My Life and the Beautiful Game (Doubleday) carries the sentence in a first-person World Cup passage, worded “the more difficult a victory.” It surfaces in the Internet Archive’s full-text index ↗ in both the 1977 first edition ↗ and the 2007 reissue.

1991–93 — the anthologies. Howard E. Ferguson’s The Edge (Getting the Edge Co., 1991) ↗ and Michael Lynberg’s Winning! (Doubleday, 1993) ↗ both turn up in the same phrase search ↗ still printing “a victory.”

1997 — the article slips. The earliest copy found in this search with the modern “the more difficult the victory” wording is Pat Mesiti’s Attitudes and Altitudes (1997) ↗, which introduces it as something “Pele, one of the world’s greatest soccer players, once said” — with no citation. That is the form the quote sites inherited.

Today — the circular citation. Wikiquote ↗ lists the altered wording sourced only to Goodreads ↗, which in turn assigns it to Pelé: The Autobiography (2006) — a book published years after the line was already in print.
source.excerptNote: Reconstructed from four overlapping snippets returned by the Internet Archive’s full-text index of the scanned book; the same sentence is indexed in the 1977 Doubleday first edition and in the 2007 Skyhorse reissue. Both scans are lending-restricted, so no page number could be read — and none is claimed. Words are given as the OCR renders them (“Selection” is the book’s English rendering of Brazil’s Seleção).

author.name: Pelé
author.heading: Pelé really did write this one
author.metaLine: 1940–2022 · Brazilian footballer, named Athlete of the Century by the IOC in 1999
author.bio: Edson Arantes do Nascimento, universally known as Pelé, was a Brazilian forward widely regarded as one of the greatest players in the history of the game. Wikipedia records his 1,279 goals in 1,363 games as a Guinness World Record, and notes that he was named Athlete of the Century by the International Olympic Committee in 1999 and included in Time’s list of the 100 most important people of the 20th century. He told his own story in My Life and the Beautiful Game (Doubleday, 1977), written with the American novelist Robert L. Fish — the book in which this sentence actually appears.

misattribution.heading: Right man, wrong word — and the wrong book
misattribution.intro: This is not a stolen quote. Pelé wrote it. What travelled wrong is the wording and the sourcing — and both errors are now baked into the pages people cite.

items.why: The memoir reads “The more difficult a victory, the greater the happiness in winning.” Sports anthologies of the early 1990s still printed “a victory”; by the time it reached the quote sites the article had hardened into “the.” Both forms are visible side by side in a single full-text search ↗.

Goodreads files the line under Pelé’s 2006 autobiography ↗. It belongs to the earlier memoir, My Life and the Beautiful Game (Doubleday, 1977), and it was already circulating in print in Howard E. Ferguson’s The Edge (1991) ↗, long before the 2006 book existed.

English Wikiquote ↗ lists the altered wording in its general Quotes section with exactly one footnote — a link to Goodreads. A quote site citing a quote site is not a source, which is how a one-word error outlived the book it came from.
AZQuotes ↗ reproduces the line with a name and no source at all — no book, no date, no page. The template that lets genuine quotations drift is the same one that lets fabricated ones spread.

misattribution.truthLine: Pelé did write it, in his own memoir in 1977 — and you can read the sentence in context in the Doubleday first edition ↗. Just quote it the way he wrote it: a victory.

context.heading: A memoir sentence, not a motivational slogan
lead: On the quote sites this reads like a fortune-cookie aphorism — a standalone maxim about grit. In the book it is nothing of the kind. It sits mid-paragraph in Pelé’s first-person account of a World Cup match, right after he notes that a goal “ensured our continuing in the World Cup games,” and right before he describes going back to the team hotel and hearing the reaction on the radio. It is a man reflecting on a night he had just survived, not a coach handing out a slogan.

That context is also why the wording matters. “The more difficult a victory” is a working footballer talking about particular wins — this one, that one. “The more difficult the victory” flattens it into a general law. The version that conquered the internet is the flattened one.
detailsBody: The line was located by running exact-phrase searches against the Internet Archive’s full-text book index through Open Library’s search-inside ↗. Searching the popular wording (“the more difficult the victory”) returns only quotation anthologies and self-help books — no Pelé title. Searching the memoir’s actual wording (“a victory”) returns the autobiography itself, in two separate scanned editions.

Both Internet Archive copies of the memoir are lending-restricted, so the page number could not be read from the scan; only the surrounding sentences are recoverable through the search index. For that reason no page citation is claimed here.
Quote Investigator has no article on this line, and English Wikiquote’s entry carries the altered wording with a single footnote pointing at Goodreads — which is how the mis-sourcing survived.
